source.title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
source.authors: Er-Mo Hua; Xiang-Yu Hong; Bai-Ting Wu; Che Jiang; Hao-Zheng Hou; Yi-Cheng Gu; Han Wang; Qi Zeng; Ming Zhang; Ning Ding; Qi-Peng Guo; You-Bang Sun; Biqing Qi; Bo-Wen Zhou

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It compares language-model loss across controlled expert-topology changes at matched parameter or compute budgets, bearing on V4, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law relationships.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws and uses a compute-optimal vanilla configuration as its baseline, but does not test power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its own loss comparisons across architecture variants bear on V4. Downstream benchmark scores and expert-redundancy measurements are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study does not test V4 directly. It trains MoE language models with different cross-layer expert-sharing topologies at fixed stored routed-expert count (128×L) and fixed FLOPs, then compares their loss. That is a new setting (MoE expert topology) with a result on whether architecture details at fixed parameter count change loss only slightly. Every variant's loss stays within about 1% of Vanilla.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that cross-layer Meta Experts reduce expert redundancy and cross-entropy loss. They also claim higher downstream accuracy, though Table 1 is mixed per dataset. At fixed activation and granularity, Meta-Expert models match Vanilla MoE with 70–80% of experts. Theoretically, shared experts give bidirectional residual pathways across depth. The authors do not address scaling laws as such.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares MoE expert-sharing architectures and their loss, rather than fitting scaling-law curves or testing extrapolation and compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss varies with Meta/Local ratios and expert topology; the text also reports that preferred topology depends on model depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Meta-Expert models match Vanilla loss with 70–80% of experts (75–90% of parameters) at iso-FLOPs, and the saving grows with depth and compute (Fig 1, param-reduction ablation).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-layer expert sharing shifts the effective-parameter scaling of MoE language models, with a saving that grows with scale.

record.problems: Loss comparisons are presented primarily in figures without tabulated values or uncertainty estimates. The scaling ladder is a single model family and does not fit power laws.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream benchmark scores and expert-redundancy results were left out because they do not measure the loss behavior named by V4. The parameter-reduction ablation changes stored parameter count, so it does not address V4's fixed-parameter comparison.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
The compute-optimal vanilla configuration is taken from prior practice and the authors' own sweep, but no N/D allocation is fitted or reported.
Depth, width and aspect ratio at fixed parameter count are not varied; depth and width are scaled jointly across rungs. Only MoE expert-sharing topology is varied, in a single model family.
No other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream scores are reported for one scale only, with no scaling relation.
No fitted exponents and no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The V4 verdict rests on loss-ratio ranges read from figure axes, not tabulated numbers, and no uncertainty is reported. The reported loss is training loss over the final ten steps, not held-out loss. The differences are small but systematic and widen with compute (R5). This is still within 'slight', but researchers should note the effect is not shown to stay small beyond 2.4e20 FLOPs. The architecture axis tested (expert sharing) is narrower than V4's depth/width focus. Downstream results (Table 1) are single-scale and excluded from rows.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss relationships in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token split and its growth with compute.
The study tests expert topology and sharing choices at controlled budgets, not a broad range of depth and width changes or all architecture details.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: 2B-A0.5B model
rows.operation_detail: Compared Meta/Local expert proportions and per-layer activation proportions with total expert count and activated count held fixed.
rows.note: The paper states that a higher total Meta-Expert proportion consistently lowers loss; higher activation share for Local Experts degrades loss. The plotted values are not tabulated.
rows.check: The value is not tabulated, but the Fig 4 axis bounds the loss ratios to about 0.996–1.002. Record this range instead of leaving the value as 'figure only'.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-style MoE scaling ladder
rows.size_stated: Depths 12, 16, 20, and 24; widths vary by depth
rows.operation_detail: Compared Meta/Local total-number ratios across training-compute rungs with per-layer activation fixed at 4 Meta and 4 Local experts.
rows.note: The text says the 75% Meta ratio is the best partial-Meta setting at every compute budget, while pure Meta is slightly better. Individual loss values are shown in the figure, not tabulated.
rows.check: The Fig 5 axis bounds the loss ratios to about 0.994–1.000 across four rungs (7.1e18–2.4e20 FLOPs). The row should note that the 100% Meta (pure-Meta) variant is also plotted. The loss is training loss averaged over the final 10 steps, not held-out loss.

source_check.problem: Retain figure only. Figure 5 also includes the pure-Meta variant, which activates 8 Meta and 0 Local experts; partial-Meta variants activate 4+4.

rows.subject: 2B-A0.5B model
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer allocations with Local-Experts-only boundary layers and Meta-Expert pools divided into looped sub-pools.

conditions.value: Local-only first and/or last 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers; Meta pools looped in 2, 4, or 8 sub-pools, chunked or interleaved

rows.note: Most topology interventions generally degrade loss; the text identifies slight improvements for restricting only the first and last two layers to Local Experts or looping Meta Experts twice. Individual values are not tabulated.
rows.check: The reader marked this partial because most topology interventions degrade loss relative to MR75. For V4, the relevant fact is that every Fig 6 variant stays within roughly 0.994–1.000 of Vanilla, a small effect. So V4 is observed, not partial.

source_check.problem: Retain figure only. Degradation is relative to the partial-Meta starting configuration, so it does not itself contradict V4.

tranche.reason: The study supplies controlled loss comparisons in a new architectural setting: cross-layer expert sharing in hybrid-attention MoE language models.

source_check.notes: Keep all five values as figure only; axis ticks do not establish measured minima or maxima. These comparisons concern training loss and expert topology; they do not establish held-out power-law scaling or invariance to depth and width.

statements.correction: Loss ratios: figure only; numerical extrema not stated. Ladder loss: training language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten steps. Within each rung: fixed 128×L routed-expert budget and top-8 activation. Capability evaluation: 6B-A1.6B models trained on 200B tokens, Section 3.4 and Table 1.
statements.problem: The 0.990–1.002 interval is assembled from figure-axis labels; the supplied text does not report it as the measured range across variants. The architectural controls and capability check are supported.
